चार दिनों की तपन ने उड़ा दी थी रातों की नींद
रानीगंज प्रखंड और आसपास के इलाकों में बीते चार दिनों से स्थिति काफी विकट बनी हुई थी:
- घर से निकलना हुआ था मुश्किल: सुबह से ही कड़क धूप निकल आने के कारण दोपहर में सड़कों और बाजारों में सन्नाटा पसर जाता था.
- उमस से बेहाल थे लोग: तेज धूप और हवा में बढ़ी नमी (Humidity) के कारण लोगों का रात में भी चैन से सोना दुश्वार हो गया था. अचानक बढ़े तापमान ने क्षेत्रवासियों को भीषण गर्मी का अहसास करा दिया था.
सोमवार सुबह हुई बारिश से सुहाना हुआ मौसम
सोमवार की सुबह आसमान में काले बादलों ने डेरा डाला और झमाझम बारिश शुरू हो गई:
- तापमान में गिरावट: बारिश होने से हवा में ठंडक घुल गई, जिससे पिछले चार दिनों से तप रहे इलाकों में लोगों ने राहत की सांस ली.
- जनजीवन को मिली राहत: सुबह-सुबह हुई इस वर्षा से मौसम खुशनुमा हो गया. मॉर्निंग वॉक पर निकले लोगों और जरूरी काम से घर से बाहर जाने वाले नागरिकों को इस सुहावने मौसम से काफी सहूलियत महसूस हुई.

अमृतसर में दो दिन से बिजली गुल, गर्मी से बेहाल लोगों ने सड़क पर लगाया जाम
भीषण गर्मी के बीच लगातार बिजली कटौती से परेशान लोगों का गुस्सा रविवार को फूट पड़ा। जोड़ा फाटक, मोहकमपुरा चौक, रसूलपुर कल्लर और कृष्णा नगर समेत कई इलाकों में करीब दो दिन से बिजली आपूर्ति ठप रहने के विरोध में लोग सड़क पर उतर आए और मोहकमपुरा चौक के पास धरना देकर प्रदर्शन किया। प्रदर्शन के दौरान हल्का पूर्वी से कांग्रेस नेता व पूर्व इम्प्रूवमेंट ट्रस्ट चेयरमैन दिनेश बस्सी अपने बेटे वंश बस्सी और पार्षद छिंदर बिड़लान के साथ लोगों के बीच धरने पर बैठ गए।
प्रदर्शनकारियों ने बिजली विभाग और पंजाब सरकार के खिलाफ नारेबाजी करते हुए आरोप लगाया कि क्षेत्र की विधायक जीवनजोत कौर ने उनकी समस्याओं की अनदेखी की। लोगों का कहना था कि शनिवार रात से बिजली बंद है, जिससे पानी की आपूर्ति भी प्रभावित हो गई है। भीषण गर्मी में बच्चों, बुजुर्गों और महिलाओं को सबसे अधिक परेशानी झेलनी पड़ रही है।
स्थानीय निवासी साहिल, प्रिंस और गुरदेव सिंह ने कहा कि मजबूरी में उन्हें सड़क पर उतरना पड़ा है। उन्होंने चेतावनी दी कि बिजली बहाल होने तक धरना जारी रहेगा। दिनेश बस्सी ने कहा कि वह जनता के साथ हैं और जब तक लोग धरने पर बैठे रहेंगे, वह भी वहीं रहेंगे। वहीं पार्षद छिंदर बिड़लान ने आम आदमी पार्टी सरकार पर लोगों की समस्याओं की अनदेखी करने का आरोप लगाया।
सूचना मिलने पर थाना प्रभारी मौके पर पहुंचे और प्रदर्शनकारियों को समझाकर धरना समाप्त कराने का प्रयास किया। उन्होंने जल्द बिजली आपूर्ति बहाल कराने का आश्वासन दिया, लेकिन लोगों ने स्पष्ट कर दिया कि बिजली आने तक उनका प्रदर्शन जारी रहेगा।

मिर्जापुर। सावन से पहले मौसम की बेरुखी रविवार को भी जारी रही। तेज धूप और उमस भरी गर्मी ने लोगों की मुश्किलें बढ़ा दीं। 24 घंटे में अधिकतम तापमान एक डिग्री बढ़कर 35 डिग्री सेल्सियस पहुंच गया, जबकि न्यूनतम तापमान 26 डिग्री सेल्सियस पर स्थिर रहा। दोपहर के समय गर्मी का असर ऐसा रहा कि प्रमुख बाजारों, चौराहों और तिराहों पर चहल-पहल थम गई। लोग केवल जरूरी काम से निकले।

Why India Needs To Record Heatwave Mortality Better
Different departments have different estimates, but a national figure is missing
Chhatarpur, Madhya Pradesh: Between March 2023 and July 2024, Madhya Pradesh recorded 12,765 suspected heatstroke cases—the highest in India—but only 18 deaths were officially reported, government data show. Similarly, in Uttar Pradesh during the same period, 5,731 suspected cases of heatstroke were recorded, and 52 cases of death due to heatstroke were registered. Several other states also show similar patterns.
We need to know how many of the 12,765 people survived in Madhya Pradesh, how many died and of what causes, said Dileep Mavalankar, distinguished professor of public health and former director of the Indian Institute of Public Health, Gandhinagar. "Are all the remaining people—except for the 18 who died—alive? If not, what are the causes of death for the other people who died?"
India’s heatwave death reporting is scattered, with different official sources measuring differently.
In 2024, the latest year for which the National Crime Records Bureau has data, the Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India report showed 1,832 heat/sunstroke deaths. That same year, the National Centre for Disease Control under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare recorded 161 confirmed heatstroke deaths through the National Heat-Related Illness and Death Surveillance. The India Meteorological Department, which collates numbers from reports in the media and of government disaster management authorities, recorded 389 heatwave deaths.
In Europe, for instance, EuroMOMO—a mortality monitoring effort supported by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control—reported 10,000 excess deaths during the June heatwave.
The absence of a national database on heat-related mortality "weakens planning, hides the true scale of the crisis, and makes accountability much harder", Apekshita Varshney, founder of Heat Watch, a research and advocacy non-profit, explained. "It also means we are almost certainly underestimating both the human toll and the economic cost of extreme heat."
“Climate-driven changes in temperature could contribute to approximately 430,000 additional deaths annually by 2050,” research from the Climate Impact Lab, at the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago, shows. Many regions most impacted also lack the energy needed to adapt—with 10 times more deaths occurring in poor countries by 2050 than in wealthier countries, researchers found.
Unless emissions are reduced aggressively, there could be, in the worst-case scenario, 221 extra global heat deaths per 100,000 people every year, as ISignal reported in September 2020. The best case scenario would still see 73 extra deaths per 100,000—equal to the number of people who die every year of several major infectious diseases combined.
We have reached out to the Union government and state government for comment. We will update this story when we receive a response.
A case of contested cause of death
On the morning of June 5, 40-year-old Subhan Ahmed was found unconscious, with his hands on the graves of his wife and son, in Charkhari town of Uttar Pradesh's Mahoba district. He was later taken to a hospital, where doctors declared him dead. It all started 11 days earlier.
May 25 was a hot day in Harpalpur in Madhya Pradesh’s Chhatarpur district. Six-year-old Hasnain spent the day playing, both outdoors and within their home. With Eid around the corner, his brother Saif Mansouri took him to get a haircut at around 3.30 p.m. By 6 p.m., the brother received a call informing him that Hasnain had taken ill.
Hasnain had started vomiting and had diarrhoea. "We immediately took him to the nearby private hospital, Life Health Care," said Wasir Mohammed, Hasnain's 62-year-old grandfather.
"Symptoms of cyanosis had started appearing in the child, his body parts were turning blue, and his eyes were rolling upwards," explained Yogendra Kumar Dixit, doctor at Life Health Care. They advised taking him to the Civil Hospital in Naugaon, 32 km away.
"Cyanosis occurs when the heart or lungs fail and circulation collapses," Mavalankar explained.
Meanwhile, his mother Razia Khatoon, 35, also took ill. "She began feeling anxious and dizzy," Mohammed said. At the Naugaon Civil Hospital, doctors recorded Hasnain as critically ill on arrival, noting vomiting, severe pallor, lethargy and poor circulation. Hospital records also documented a "poor prognosis".
"The nurse said that Hasnain was facing a lack of blood in his body and his oxygen level was also dropping. Both Razia and Hasnain were referred to the district hospital," Mohammed said. At the district hospital in Chhatarpur, doctors declared both the mother and son dead on arrival. The family members believe that Hasnain died due to heatstroke and his mother Razia Khatoon died of a heart attack from shock.
However, Chhatarpur Chief Medical and Health Officer (CMHO) Rajendra Kumar Gupta denied the possibility of death due to the heatwave. Citing the referral letter from Naugaon Civil Hospital, he said Hasnain had eaten watermelon and had had a cold drink that day. "I have been told that the cause of the worsening condition could be food poisoning. The real cause of death will be known only after the viscera report arrives," Gupta said.
The post-mortem report did not establish a definitive cause of death. The autopsy surgeon gave a provisional opinion that Hasnain's death "may be due to cardiorespiratory failure" and stated that a final conclusion would depend on forensic, chemical and histopathological examination of preserved tissue samples.
Mavalankar said food poisoning has an average mortality rate of less than 1%. In most cases, the body recovers with intravenous fluids and antibiotics. "If food poisoning was the cause of death, it would be an even greater tragedy and big failure of the health system," he added. "It would mean the contamination was extraordinarily severe. Samples of the watermelon, cold drink, and household water should have been tested."
The physiology of heatwave deaths
"The human body is like a chemistry lab, with every cell carrying out reactions that function best at 37°C," Mavalankar explained. "When extreme heat pushes body temperature higher, those reactions falter. Cells begin to die. In the brain, this leads to unconsciousness; in the kidneys, to renal failure; in the heart, to cardiac failure. Ultimately, multiple organ failure can occur.”
In Hasnain's case, he said, “A child playing outdoors in severe heat, already physically active, can see their internal temperature rise to fatal levels. We must ask why the heart stopped—was it heat, or toxins?"
Heat stroke deaths can be classified as direct deaths (due to exertion under direct sunlight) and indirect or non-exertional deaths (people who suffer a heat stroke due to high ambient temperature--such as those trapped inside homes with high room temperatures), as ISignal had explained in June 2020.
“If you just look for medically certified heat stroke deaths, they account for only 10% of total deaths due to heat waves,” Mavalankar had told us in 2020, describing heat wave deaths as an iceberg: “90% [which are indirect deaths] is not visible.”
"Hospital data alone is not enough," he added. "Many deaths occur at home, in fields, or at workplaces. To measure heatwave mortality accurately, daily death counts must be recorded at cemeteries and cremation grounds and health experts should find out proper causes for these recorded deaths. India has not developed such a system since Independence."
At the district level, health departments have very few public health specialists, which is another problem, said Mavalankar. He argues that the government should also appoint demographers in every vulnerable district to analyse heatwave mortality statistics.
Gaps in preparedness
The National Centre for Disease Control's 2026 heatwave advisory called on state health departments to prepare hospitals and primary healthcare facilities for extreme heat. Health facilities must ensure adequate stocks of oral rehydration solutions (ORS), intravenous fluids, essential medicines, ice packs, etc.
It said secondary and tertiary healthcare facilities should establish heatstroke management units, and ensure “active, external cooling strategies that can be used for rapid and efficient cooling of patients at health facilities and field levels”.
In addition, it called for identification and procurement of resources at primary health facilities and for ambulances “to ensure on-site emergency and rapid cooling of severe heat-related illness patients in line with Cool First, Transport Second strategy”.
The Naugaon Civil Hospital, where Hasnain and Razia Khatoon were taken from the nearby private hospital, did not have a separate heat stroke ward when this writer visited on June 10. A senior nurse posted in the hospital cited staff shortage, and explained that patients with symptoms of heat stroke are admitted to and treated in the male or female wards.
When the mother and son were referred to the District Hospital, Saif Mansouri said they had to wait 20 minutes for an ambulance. On June 9, a local newspaper in Chhatarpur reported that 15 of the 25 ambulances in the district were out of order for several months. CMHO Gupta acknowledged the issue, and said the state outsources ambulance services and that he had informed senior officials about the shortage.
At the Chhatarpur District Hospital, where the mother and son were pronounced dead on arrival, the daycare centre was being used as a heat-stroke ward when this writer visited on June 10. The eight-bed ward had ceiling fans and a cooler, which was switched off at the time. Guidelines call on health facilities to ensure “general cooling appliances in waiting and patient treatment area and their functioning”.
Senior nursing officer Sunita Dhruv said the ward was being used to provide daycare facilities, and that in-patients were treated in the medicine ward. Sharad Mishra, MD medicine specialist at the District Hospital, said the medicine ward and the intensive care unit had beds reserved for heat stroke patients.
“ORS counters have been set up in the out-patient medicine distribution centre,” Mishra explained, adding that it is children and the elderly who are most affected by heatwaves. “We also counsel the family members of patients for protection against heatwaves,” he said.
“Hospitals in heatwave‑vulnerable districts must be equipped with ice packs and bathtubs for rapid cooling,” said Mavalankar. “Treatment must begin within 30 minutes; delays can cause permanent damage." CMHO Gupta confirmed that the District Hospital was using ice-packs for patients.
"With proper knowledge and training, even remote primary health centers can manage heatstroke, but awareness is lacking,” Mavalankar added. “People often fail to recognise heatstroke, and diagnosis is reduced to listing symptoms like fever or vomiting without identifying the underlying cause.”
"These gaps are unfortunately reflective of larger weaknesses in how India is preparing for heat,” Varshney said, adding that their studies have found that preparedness breaks down at the level of frontline implementation—whether that is training, staffing, access to care, or basic last-mile systems. “What matters is not just whether a plan has been notified, but whether health systems, district administrations, and local facilities are actually equipped to act when temperatures rise," she added.
"This year has already been record‑breaking. Ahmedabad endured forty days above 40°C. Next year is expected to be even hotter due to El Niño, with water scarcity compounding the crisis as rainfall is predicted to be below normal," said Mavalankar. District‑level Heat Action Plans must be implemented, with alerts announced much like curfews, and hospitals prepared for rapid treatment, he added, explaining how Ahmedabad avoided an estimated 1,190 deaths annually through effective implementation of its Heat Action Plan.
"Looking at the 2026 heatwave season, the biggest success was that heat became harder to ignore in public health and disaster management conversations,” Varshney said. “The biggest failure was that awareness did not translate into consistent, practical protection."

The Ministry of the Interior and Safety raised the national heat wave warning level to “severe,” its highest level, at 3 p.m. Monday. It also activated the Central Disaster and Safety Countermeasures Headquarters, the government’s top-level emergency response mechanism.
“Scorching heat has spread nationwide the moment monsoon season ended,” Interior Minister Yun Ho-jung, head of the emergency response body, said at a government meeting in Seoul. “The situation is extremely serious.”
Heat wave advisories are in effect across most of the country, with hot weather and tropical nights expected to continue, according to the Korea Meteorological Administration.Parts of the southeastern region that saw little rainfall are now under an emergency heat wave warning, a tier higher than standard advisories.
“We will mount an all-out government response and strengthen safety measures for high-risk groups, including vulnerable residents and outdoor workers,” Yun said.
He directed government agencies and local authorities to prioritize public safety and focus their response on conditions on the ground.
Officials plan to step up monitoring for residents of cramped housing units, the unhoused people and others vulnerable to extreme heat. They will inspect workplaces with outdoor operations for compliance with safety rules. Village leaders and volunteer disaster-prevention teams will join the ministry in checking on older farmers and urging them to avoid outdoor activity.
Authorities will inspect cooling shelters to confirm they remain open to the public and may expand operating hours if tropical nights continue. Livestock and fish farms are set to receive support installing equipment to prevent heat damage.
Officials will be dispatched to areas under emergency heat wave warnings to oversee local response efforts. Agencies must follow the ministry’s heat wave safety guidelines by shortening monitoring cycles for vulnerable residents and rescheduling outdoor events where necessary. Roads, railways and other infrastructure face inspection to prevent disruptions from power outages.
“People should drink plenty of water and rest during the hottest hours of the day,” Yun said. “Those in areas under emergency heat wave warnings should immediately stop outdoor activities and move somewhere cool.”

For the study, the researchers surveyed a nationally representative sample of 1,950 adults across the UK about how they perceived impacts of the heatwave on working hours, ability to sleep and any changes to how they travelled to work or their working environment. The survey related to the week beginning 22 June 2026.
Elizabeth Robinson and Shouro Dasgupta were able to estimate the economic cost, in terms of lost output caused by the heatwave, derived from workers’ responses about adjustments they made to their working hours. The impact of £1 billion-plus in lost output is on top of the negative impacts on workers’ health and increased pressure on health services.
They found that the “average reported reduction in hours worked across the week was 0.47 hours”. Those working in jobs more highly exposed to heat and that are physically demanding, in sectors such as construction and agriculture, reduced their hours by more than those working in low-exposure and physically undemanding jobs such as academia.
Findings from the survey show 3.6% of respondents, equivalent to approximately 1.25 million workers in the population, did not work at all that week because of the heat. This is equivalent to an additional 8 million lost hours, at an estimated cost to the economy of £0.38 billion.
87% of workers reported at least one health-related impact during the week of 22 June 2026, ranging from disrupted sleep and being more tired at work through to a small number of workers reporting more extreme symptoms including dizziness or fainting and a faster heartbeat.
The survey also found that 5% of respondents sought medical attention and around 3% reported an accident or injury at work during that week, and around two-thirds of them felt it was linked to the weather. Women, those aged under 35 and people with existing health conditions were the groups most likely to report that their health was harmed.
Elizabeth Robinson, Director of the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, said: “Our findings point to a country that remains insufficiently adapted to the changing climate.
“The Government cannot continue to ignore extreme heat. Unless it acts now, and makes workplaces safer, we are likely to see growing impacts on workers’ productivity, health, and the economy.”
Shouro Dasgupta, Environmental Economist at CMCC and Visiting Senior Fellow at the Grantham Research Institute , said:
“While £1 billion is lost overall, the greatest effects are borne by outdoor workers and those in physically demanding jobs, many of whom are among the lowest paid in the labour force.
“Extreme heat is widening existing inequalities in the labour force.”

It’s a sweet little town, Arcachon. Clinging to the long French Atlantic coast, adorned with Victorian villas and pretty flowerbeds, it reminds me oddly of the English town of Bournemouth. By which I mean: Bournemouth before it was ruined. As such, it’s the kind of place that usually calls for a return visit. I am sure for many French people it is a holiday regular – “ahh, shall we do Arcachon again? Mais oui, we can try that new oyster cabin.” But right now I seriously wonder if anyone will want to return to Arcachon, ever.
The reasons are twofold. Firstly, the news is full of searing images: of people fleeing the wildfires on Cap Ferret, and being ferried, like wartime evacuees, across the bay to Arcachon after a summer of repeated heatwaves. Secondly, several weeks ago I personally experienced the worst of those heatwaves, in and around Arcachon, and it changed my mind about the emotional impact of climate change.
My torrid holiday from hell began in green, bucolic Aveyron, where I was on assignment. Everything was so pleasant and as the official trip came to an end I thought: why not extend the adventure? My calendar was empty, I already had a hired car and I was keen to explore a part of France I’ve never seen before – the French Atlantic coast between Brittany and Bayonne.
The only fly in the ointment was the weather forecast. When I turned to my sensible AI – NinaGPT – to construct a coastal itinerary, she kept saying “Are you sure you want to do this Sean, there is a heatwave coming.” I scolded her for being a nanny and laughingly reminded her I’m a travel veteran; I like hot sunny weather and I’ve been to several war zones. I set off.
Major mistake. One afternoon, parked by an Aldi west of Conques, I watched with grim amazement as the thermometer in my car registered the intensifying heat: 116F, 118F, 120F. I actually took photographs. It was surely not that hot in reality: car thermometers are unreliable, especially if you’re sitting on baked tarmac. Nonetheless it was indicative of the heat dome settling over France. It also reminded me of the last time I’d stared at a car thermometer in wary amazement. That was in the Fish River Canyon in southern Namibia. That time, my car told me it was 115F. I took a photograph then, as well.
By the time I reached sun-struck Moissac the heatwave was near its raging peak. I quickly learned the French for this phenomenon: canicule. I also learned the sobering truth that much of provincial France lacks air conditioning. Its buildings rely on shutters, thick walls and ventilation; defenses which begin to fail above 95F. In the main square of Moissac I scurried to a shady but uncooled brasserie to bash out an article. The sweat dripped from my nose onto my laptop. Then I watched TV, as President Macron warned that the “hottest day in French history” was approaching.
It came as I arrived in Arcachon. I’d booked an apartment, right on the beach, which looked suitably modern. I figured sea breezes plus air conditioning would see me through the worst. As I pulled up, around 6pm, it was a brutal, stifling 102F. There was no sea breeze. The sea in the bay looked sad and listless, repressed by a despotic sun. To top it all off, even here there was no air conditioning.
I hadn’t checked the small print. Stupidly I’d just assumed the flat would be properly kitted out, because it was so clearly brand new. Not only did it have no air conditioning, but it also had no fans and no through breeze. It was maybe 122F in the punishment block of the bedroom. My reservation was non-refundable but I kicked up such a fuss on Booking.com’s helpline – “I could die in there” (I wasn’t joking) – they agreed to a refund. I used the money to find a grand hotel with climatisation. And then I hid.
Because that is all you can do when the thermometer soars over 104F. Hide. Shelter in place. It is like sitting out an air raid, or a hurricane, except it goes on for longer. Every time I did venture out, I got an instant pounding headache and I hurried back inside.
It was a truly horrible experience, and I write as someone who has been through severe heat. I’ve been in Luxor, Egypt when it hit 109F, I’ve been in Death Valley, Eastern California during similar. Somehow, they were more tolerable than Arcachon, France during the recent canicule. Perhaps because you expect great heat in deserts but not in the suburbs of Bordeaux; perhaps because the proximity of the sea added humidity.
I’ve had just one experience which compares to what happened in France, in the Danakil Depression, Ethiopia. I arrived at dusk in a village of mud huts, ready to climb the famous, lava-lake volcano of Erta Ale. There it was about 108F at 6pm – similar to southwest France, recently. But it’s not just the temperature that echoed: in both places I had the sensation of being trapped and tormented. Of suffering inescapably. And the mud huts had no air conditioning.
The obvious question arises. If these heatwaves continue, and worsen, what will they do to Europe, and European life? No one can be certain, but I remember my charming, capricious Auntie Lois, who spent her life shifting nervously around the world. At one point she fled Los Angeles after an earthquake. At the time I put it down to her highly-strung nature; an over-reaction. And yet I now think of her explanation, “The earthquake changed the way I felt about California. I felt like my home was turning on me, that the ground beneath me couldn’t be trusted.”
Perhaps Europe will be fine, we will briskly adapt – and install air conditioning everywhere. That’s what I used to believe. But now I am not sure. In a breakthrough that could reshape the future of aerospace and advanced engineering, researchers in China have developed a new metal alloy capable of maintaining its strength at temperatures as high as 2,400 degrees Celsius.
The innovation addresses one of the biggest challenges in materials science—creating metals that remain structurally stable under extreme heat while continuing to bear heavy mechanical loads.
Already known for its exceptionally high melting point
The research, led by a team from Xi’an Jiaotong University, centres on a specially engineered tantalum-based alloy. Tantalum is already known for its exceptionally high melting point of nearly 3,000°C, making it one of the most heat-resistant metals available. However, even tantalum alloys have traditionally suffered from a loss of strength at very high temperatures. The Chinese researchers claim to have overcome this limitation by designing an alloy with an optimized internal microstructure that resists deformation even in extreme thermal environments.
Modern technologies such as hypersonic aircraft, reusable spacecraft, advanced rocket engines and next-generation nuclear reactors require materials that can survive enormous temperatures without weakening. Conventional high-performance alloys, including nickel-based superalloys widely used in jet engines, begin to lose their mechanical strength as temperatures approach 2,000°C.
Newly developed alloy remains capable of supporting heavy loads
The newly developed alloy reportedly remains capable of supporting heavy loads at temperatures up to 2,400°C, representing a significant improvement over existing high-temperature structural materials.
Metals generally become softer as temperatures rise because their internal crystal structures become more mobile. Once temperatures exceed roughly 60% of a metal’s melting point, atoms can move more freely, causing the material to deform under stress.
According to the researchers, the new tantalum alloy has been engineered with a carefully controlled microscopic structure that slows this process. By stabilising the material’s internal arrangement, the alloy retains its strength even under conditions that would normally weaken conventional metals.
The findings were published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature, highlighting the scientific significance of the work.
If the material performs similarly outside laboratory conditions, it could have wide-ranging industrial applications, including hypersonic missile and aircraft components, rocket nozzles and combustion chambers, spacecraft thermal protection systems, advanced gas turbines, and nuclear reactor components.
The ability to operate safely at such extreme temperatures could improve engine efficiency, extend component lifespan and reduce cooling requirements in demanding engineering environments.
While the laboratory results are promising, commercial adoption will require further testing. Scientists must demonstrate that the alloy can be manufactured economically, withstand repeated heating and cooling cycles, resist oxidation and corrosion, and perform reliably over long service periods.
Tantalum is also an expensive metal, meaning large-scale industrial use will depend on whether production costs can be reduced without compromising performance.
The development reflects the growing pace of innovation in advanced materials research. As countries compete to build faster aircraft, more efficient space vehicles and safer nuclear technologies, breakthroughs in high-temperature alloys are becoming increasingly important.

[Sportschosun reporter Jang Jong-ho] In summer, the number of patients visiting emergency rooms not only for heat-related illnesses but also for cerebrovascular and cardiovascular diseases increases.
In particular, arrhythmia is one of the conditions most affected by heat and dehydration. It can occur not only in people with existing heart disease, high blood pressure, or heart failure, but also in younger adults, so extra caution is needed.
The biggest reason heatwaves raise the risk of arrhythmia is dehydration. When people sweat heavily in hot weather, the amount of water in the blood decreases, which can reduce blood volume and lower blood pressure. To compensate, the heart beats faster, and the balance of the autonomic nervous system is disrupted, making the heart's electrical signals unstable. In the process, arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation or tachycardia can develop, or existing arrhythmias can worsen. Patients taking diuretics and older adults are especially prone to dehydration, so they need to pay even closer attention to hydration during the summer.
Arrhythmia is a condition in which the heart fails to maintain a normal rhythm and beats too fast, too slowly, or irregularly. It includes a wide range of types, from relatively common arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation to life-threatening ones such as ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. Ventricular fibrillation is the most dangerous form, as the heart cannot pump blood properly and it can lead to cardiac arrest and sudden death.
Arrhythmia often develops as a result of aging, but the number of younger patients has also been steadily rising in recent years.
In addition to congenital genetic disorders and heart diseases such as myocardial infarction, cardiomyopathy, and valvular disease, chronic stress, lack of sleep, excessive caffeine and energy drink consumption, heavy drinking, and smoking can all affect the autonomic nervous system and the heart's electrical signals, increasing the risk of arrhythmia.
Symptoms also vary. The most common signs are palpitations or the sensation of an irregular pulse, but dizziness, shortness of breath, chest pain, and fatigue can also occur. In particular, sudden loss of consciousness, or syncope, may be an important warning sign of a cardiac arrhythmia. If a person faints during exercise or while lying down without any clear reason, experiences severe palpitations or chest pain before fainting, or has a family member who suffered sudden death at a young age, a specialized cardiac evaluation is essential.
The most important part of diagnosing arrhythmia is confirming the electrocardiogram at the moment symptoms appear. However, because arrhythmias are often temporary, they are not always detected in a standard ECG test. For this reason, patch-type ECG monitors attached to the skin are now used to record heart rhythm for one to two weeks. For patients whose symptoms occur only rarely, an implantable loop recorder inserted under the skin may be used to monitor the ECG for years and identify the cause. Depending on the case, echocardiography, cardiac MRI, exercise stress testing, and genetic testing may also be performed to determine the underlying cause.
Treatment depends on the type and cause of the arrhythmia. Bradyarrhythmias, in which the heart rate is too slow and fainting occurs repeatedly, can be managed with a pacemaker to maintain a normal rhythm. On the other hand, malignant arrhythmias such as ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia are treated with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), which delivers an electric shock as soon as a dangerous arrhythmia occurs to restore a normal rhythm. Atrial fibrillation is treated with medication as well as radiofrequency ablation or cryoballoon ablation. More recently, Pulse Field Ablation (PFA), which selectively treats only cardiac tissue, has drawn attention as a new treatment that can reduce damage to surrounding tissue and shorten procedure time.
To prevent arrhythmia during heatwaves, it is best to drink enough water before feeling thirsty and avoid caffeinated drinks and excessive alcohol. Exercise should be done in the cooler morning or evening hours, within a reasonable range, and sudden temperature differences between indoors and outdoors should also be minimized. Patients with high blood pressure or heart disease should check their blood pressure and pulse regularly and should not stop taking their medication on their own.
Professor Choi Young of the Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Hospital at The Catholic University of Korea Seoul St. Mary's Hospital's Cardiology Department said, "Arrhythmia may end with simple palpitations, but some cases can lead to cardiac arrest and sudden death," adding, "Especially in summer, when dehydration and autonomic nervous system changes become more severe because of the heat, people should not dismiss symptoms lightly. If repeated palpitations, fainting, chest pain, or shortness of breath occur, it is most important to seek prompt specialist care and identify the exact cause."

Nashville doctor shares heat exhaustion warning as temperatures soar
A Nashville doctor who helps safeguard music lovers during steamy summer festivals shared key tips on avoiding heat exhaustion at events and elsewhere to safeguard kids, adults and pets.
With Nashville-area temperatures expected to stay in the 90s for much of the final week of July, knowing how to recognize and treat heat exhaustion and heat stroke could be critical, said Dr. Ashley Panas, chief flight physician with Vanderbilt University Medical Center's LifeFlight. Panas has helped staff medical services during racing events at Nashville Superspeedway, CMA Fest and events at Nissan Stadium that bring crowds, fun and, often, heat-related illness.
"We certainly see a lot of heat-related illness," Panas said. "Early illnesses can be fairly minor but can also be fairly extreme. Heat stroke is life threatening and that's when your body core temperature starts to affect your vital organs."
Young children and the elderly are at higher risk, but healthy young adults also can become sick from the heat, she said.
Heat exhaustion symptoms include heavy sweating; headache; dizziness; fatigue; nausea or vomiting; rapid heart rate and intense thirst. Meanwhile, heat stroke comes with a body temperature of 103 degrees or higher; confusion or disorientation; slurred speech; hot, red skin and fainting, seizures or loss of consciousness.
"All ages are susceptible to heat stroke," especially when exercising in the heat, she said.
A few simple steps can keep the good times going and lessen the risks of injury.
What to do before an outdoor concert or event
Start early by drinking plenty of water the day before you plan to be outside in the heat so your body is hydrated, the doctor said.
Otherwise, if you start out dehydrated, you're going to be more susceptible of heat illness at the event.
Staying safe at Nashville festivals
Panas advised that workers and concertgoers make a mental note of the location of the medical tent as they enter the event just in case.
It's important to drink lots of water and beverages with electrolytes, she said.
Some venues will offer cooling stations with shade and water.
If alcohol is consumed, it's important to drink moderately because it can be a double-whammy, causing someone to become dehydrated more quickly and dulling the awareness of possible heat exhaustion, the doctor said.
Signs of possible heat exhaustion
If someone starts talking nonsensically, it could be a sign of heat exhaustion, Panas said. Other signs can include headaches, nausea. muscle cramping and lightheadedness.
Someone in danger of overheating may turn red or may become pale an clammy, Panas said.
Someone suffering a heat stroke might suffer a seizure or lose consciousness.
Rapid cooling
Medical teams at outdoor events have rapid cooling plans to aid victims on site before transporting them to a hospital.
"The literature in recent years has shown that if we can rapidly cool someone at the time that we identify them as a heat stroke victim, their outcomes are much better," Panas said.
The teams will move the patient to the shade and immerse them in an ice bath to lower their core temperature on site, the doctor said.
How long can you leave your pet in a hot car?
Panas advises not to leave your pet in a hot car, even with windows cracked.
Temperatures inside the car can rise quickly, endangering pets and children, according to warnings by the state Health Department.
Health experts urge drivers to routinely check front and back seats for kids and pets before leaving the car.
